ORDER
This Board received a notice of appeal from Atlantic Tide and Turnout, LLC
(Atlantic Tide)1 and docketed the appeal as IBLA 2022-111. The notice of appeal
involves a special use permit (SUP) issued by the Superintendent, Cape Cod National
Seashore, National Park Service (NPS).2 Subsequently, we received from Atlantic Tide a
statement of reasons and a petition for stay, among other documents.3
However, our jurisdiction is limited to adjudicating appeals of “decisions rendered
by Departmental officials relating to” public lands and their resources, mineral resources
in acquired and offshore lands, and surface coal mining.4 Because of our limited
jurisdiction, we may only adjudicate appeals of decisions rendered by a “Bureau or
Office” or an administrative law judge within the Office of Hearings and Appeals.5 As
reflected in our regulations, “Bureau or Office” means the Bureau of Indian Affairs, the
Bureau of Land Management, the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement
(BSEE), the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM), the Office of Natural
Resources Revenue, the Deputy Assistant Secretary – Natural Resources Revenue, “or any

KLAMATH SISKIYOU WILDLANDS ) Invasive Plant Management
CENTER )
) Affirmed
ORDER∗
Appellant Klamath Siskiyou Wildlands Center (KS Wild) filed this appeal from an
April 5, 2019, Decision issued by the Field Manager of the Bureau of Land Management’s
Lakeview District – Klamath Falls Resource Area (KFRA) in Oregon (BLM). In the
Decision, BLM broadened the scope of the KFRA’s weed management program from
noxious weeds to include all invasive plants, authorized additional non-herbicide direct
control methods, and increased the number of herbicides available for use from 4 to 17.
KS Wild alleges that BLM’s National Environmental Policy Act analysis is deficient
in multiple respects, that the Decision is inconsistent with the governing resource
management plan, and that BLM failed to comply with the Endangered Species Act. For
the reasons explained below, we find that KS Wild has not met its burden to show error
in BLM’s Decision and accordingly affirm.
BACKGROUND
A. BLM’s Decision
BLM’s Decision revises its program for the control of invasive plants using
specified herbicide and non-herbicide methods throughout the KFRA (with the exception
of the Tunnel Creek Area of Critical Environmental Concern, where no treatments are
authorized), which encompasses approximately 225,000 acres in Klamath County,
Oregon.1 Invasive plants are “nonnative aggressive plants with the potential to cause

significant damage to native ecosystems and/or cause significant economic losses.”2 Prior
to the Decision, the KFRA had managed weeds pursuant to a 1993 Integrated Weed
Management Plan and Environmental Assessment and Decision Record (the 1993 Plan).3
The 1993 Plan authorized control of only noxious weeds, a subset of invasive plants that
are county, State, or Federally listed as injurious to public health, agriculture, recreation,
wildlife, or public or private property.4 Under the 1993 Plan, authorized non-herbicide
methods included hand-pulling and competitive seeding and planting, and authorized
herbicides included 2,4-D, glyphosate, dicamba, and picloram.5
BLM decided to update and expand the program to authorize treatment methods
that are “generally more selective, provide better control, and have fewer adverse
environmental effects.”6 It explained that despite efforts under the prior program,
noxious weeds were continuing to spread at an estimated rate of 12 percent per year,
and that more selective herbicides were available to treat invasive plants.7 In its
Decision, BLM expanded the list of permissible non-herbicide treatment methods to
include targeted grazing, biological control agents, competitive seeding and planting,
propane torch spot treatments, broadcast burning, and mechanical methods such as
chainsaws and string trimmers.8 The herbicides authorized under the revised program
include 2,4-D, aminopyralid, chlorsulfuron, clopyralid, dicamba, dicamba +
diflufenzopyr, fluroxypyr, glyphosate, imazapic, imazapyr, metsulfuron methyl, picloram,
rimsulfuron, sulfometuron methyl, triclopyr, and limited and controlled use of fluazifop-
P-butyl and Pseudomonas fluorescens.9 BLM explained that these herbicides are “more
selective in treating invasive plants” and “can be used in lower quantities and pose less
environmental and human health safety risk than the herbicides” previously utilized.10

Given the significant amount of time that had passed since BLM issued the

have been resolved or had otherwise become unnecessary to decide, among other
issues.31 In their status report, the parties jointly stated that the Decision “is being

ANALYSIS
A. Summary Affirmance is Not Warranted
Relying on Klamath-Siskiyou Wildlands Center,35 BLM argues that the Board
should summarily affirm BLM’s decision because KS Wild has merely reiterated the
arguments it raised during the NEPA process, and BLM considered and responded to
these comments in the EA Comment/Response Summary.36 In Klamath-Siskiyou
Wildlands Center, however, the Board had before it a denial of a protest to a forest
management decision.37 The Board found that where the appellant merely repeated

had failed to identify error in the decision on appeal.38 Here, there has been no separate
agency decision specifically responding to KS Wild’s arguments akin to the adjudication
of a protest or other similar process. This Board has previously declined to summarily
affirm similar BLM decisions concerning integrated invasive plant management plans in

We now turn to the merits of KS Wild’s arguments on appeal.
B. KS Wild Has Not Met Its Burden to Establish a NEPA Violation
KS Wild’s alleges that BLM’s NEPA analysis is deficient in the following respects:
1) the EA is programmatic in nature and does not adequately support the suite of actions
proposed or the Annual Treatment Plans; 2) BLM erred in using data in the NISIMS and
did not provide sufficient location and scale information to permit meaningful public
involvement; 3) BLM failed to comply with applicable adaptive management regulations;
4) the EA is biased against nonnative species and scientifically inaccurate; 5) BLM failed
to adequately analyze the impacts of aerial spraying and targeted grazing; 6) BLM erred
by authorizing the use of picloram; 7) BLM failed to consider relevant information about
glyphosate; and 8) BLM failed to adequately analyze the cumulative impacts of its action
combined with the Oregon Department of Transportation’s spraying of herbicides on
adjacent State highways.41 Before addressing these arguments, we first set forth the
governing law at the time of BLM’s Decision.
1. Legal Principles Governing National Environmental Policy Act Challenges
Section 102(2)(C) of NEPA requires Federal agencies to prepare an
Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) evaluating the potential environmental impacts
of any major Federal action significantly affecting the quality of the human
environment.42 As it did here, BLM may prepare an EA to assist its determination of

whether an EIS is required or to aid the agency’s decision-making when an EIS is
unnecessary.43 As it also did here, BLM issues a FONSI when it concludes that an EIS is
not necessary.44
An EA is “a concise public document” that includes “brief discussions” of the
“environmental impacts of the proposed action and alternatives”45 at a level of depth and
detail normally “limited to the minimum needed to determine whether there would be
significant environmental effects” from the proposed action.46 This Board has
consistently held that an “EA need not discuss the merits and drawbacks of the proposal
in exhaustive detail” as by “its nature, it is intended to be an overview of environmental
concerns, not an exhaustive study of all environmental issues”; accordingly, so long “as
an EA contains a ‘reasonably thorough discussion of . . . significant aspects of the
probable environmental consequences,’ NEPA requirements have been satisfied.”47
In evaluating the adequacy of an EA, the Board is guided by a “rule of reason”48
and will generally find that BLM has taken the requisite “hard look” when its conclusion
that no significant environmental impact exists is founded on a reasoned evaluation of
relevant factors that is documented in the record.49 Our task is not to determine whether
an EA is based upon the best scientific data or methodology available, or to resolve
scientific disagreement over those subjects, but rather to determine whether BLM’s
analysis of the available data was reasonable and provides an adequate basis for its
decision.50 An appellant challenging a BLM decision analyzed in an EA “has the burden
of demonstrating with objective proof that the decision is premised on a clear error of
law or demonstrable error of fact, or that the analysis failed to consider a substantial
environmental question of material significance to the proposed action.”51 This burden is
not satisfied by speculation, conclusory allegations unsupported by evidence, or mere
differences of opinion regarding the likelihood or significance of environmental

The fact that “an appellant has a different opinion about the likelihood or significance of

BLM is entitled to rely on the professional opinions of its technical experts
concerning matters within the realm of their expertise and which are reasonable and

demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence, error in the data, methodology,
analysis, or conclusion of the expert.55 Such opinions are entitled to considerable
deference,56 and a “mere difference of opinion, even of expert opinion, will not suffice to
show that BLM failed to fully comprehend the true nature, magnitude, or scope of the
likely impacts.”57 Ultimately, NEPA is a procedural statute that requires only full

2. KS Wild Has Not Shown that the EA is Insufficiently Detailed as a General
Matter or that BLM’s Approach of Preparing Annual Treatment Plans and
Evaluating Them Against the EA is Inconsistent with NEPA

At the outset, we find that KS Wild’s challenge to the 2019 Annual Treatment Plan

identified their adverse impacts.
We find that KS Wild has not shown error in BLM’s cumulative impacts analysis.
C. KS Wild Has Not Met Its Burden to Establish a Federal Land Policy and
Management Act Violation
1. Legal Principles Governing Federal Land Policy and Management Act
Challenges
The Federal Land Policy and Management Act requires BLM to “manage the
public lands under principles of multiple use and sustained yield, in accordance with the

management plans,” establish the allowable uses, goals, and next steps for a particular
area.184 Once a resource management plan is developed, “[a]ll future resource
management authorizations and actions . . . shall conform to the approved plan.”185 A
management action is in conformance with a land use plan if it is “specifically provided
for in the plan, or if not specifically mentioned, [is] clearly consistent with the terms,
conditions, and decisions of the approved plan or plan amendment.”186 An appellant
contending that a management action is inconsistent with a governing resource
management plan must show error in BLM’s determination that its action conforms to
the terms of the plan.187
2. Appellants Have Not Shown Error in BLM’s Determinations that the Decision
Conforms to the Governing Resource Management Plan or a Related
Injunction.
KS Wild argues that aerial spraying and subsequent planting of native species
“would substantially increase livestock forage which is prohibited by law and the [2016
Southwestern Oregon Resource Management Plan (SWORMP)].”188 KS Wild also argues
that the Decision’s authorization of targeted grazing is inconsistent with the SWORMP
because the SWORMP does not specifically list targeted grazing as an option for
managing invasive species.189 Neither of these arguments establishes error in BLM’s
Decision.
KS Wild has identified no provision of the SWORMP prohibiting BLM from
aerially spraying herbicides. The SWORMP does, however, expressly direct BLM to
control invasive species.190 In particular, it directs BLM to “[p]revent the introduction of
invasive species and the spread of existing invasive species infestations.”191 It further
directs BLM to use “manual, mechanical, cultural, chemical, and biological treatments”

in this effort.192 Herbicide application is a chemical treatment method and therefore falls
within this list.
KS Wild has also not shown that BLM’s authorization of targeted grazing to treat
invasive species is inconsistent with the SWORMP. Targeted grazing is a biological
treatment method and therefore also falls within the SWORMP’s list of tools that BLM is

the Decision does not authorize the spraying of herbicides for this purpose. Rather, it
authorizes the spraying of herbicides for the purpose of controlling invasive species. In
its Decision, BLM explained that the “combination of tools” it authorized “would be
effective on all of the invasive plant species known or suspected to occur on the KFRA, as
well as new invaders,” and as a consequence, “treatment objectives, such as reducing
infestations to below damage levels for Special Status species and special communities,
would be met more frequently and on more acres compared to the No Action

Highway 97.”197 BLM also considered an alternative involving no aerial herbicide
application but eliminated it from detailed study because without the treatment method,
“the risk of invasive annual grass rate of spread would increase following wildfires over

KFRA.”198

D. KS Wild Has Not Established an Endangered Species Act Violation
KS Wild argues that BLM “failed to consult with [FWS] about targeted grazing”
and states that the “ARBO II does not address targeted grazing.199 Presumably, KS Wild
means to assert a violation of Section 7(a)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA),
which requires agencies to consult with the United States Fish and Wildlife Service
(FWS) or the National Marine Fisheries Service to “insure that any action authorized,
funded, or carried out . . . is not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of any
endangered species or threatened species or result in the destruction or adverse
modification of [critical] habitat of such species.”200
At the time of BLM’s Decision, six Federally listed species and/or critical habitat
units were known to occur within the analysis area.201 Where a listed species may be
present in the area of a proposed action, BLM is generally directed to prepare a
Biological Assessment to evaluate the “potential effects of the action on listed . . . species
and designated . . .critical habitat and determine whether any such species or habitat are
likely to be adversely affected by the action,” and whether formal consultation is
required.202 Informal consultation is required when the proposed action may affect but is
not likely to adversely affect a species, and formal consultation is required when the
proposed action may affect and is likely to adversely affect the species.203 In the former
circumstance, the proposed action may go forward when FWS concurs in BLM’s not
likely to adversely affect determination; in the latter circumstance, the proposed action
may go forward when FWS prepares a Biological Opinion concluding that the action will
not result in jeopardy to the species.204
Prior to its Decision, BLM had consulted with FWS on numerous prior actions
involving invasive plant management, including the 2007 ROD, the 2010 ROD, and the
2016 SWORMP.205 In 2013, another consultation culminated in a Programmatic
Biological Opinion for Aquatic Restoration Activities in the States of Oregon, Washington

Contrary to KS Wild’s suggestion, BLM did not determine that the ARBO II

BLM made a “no effect” determination for these species and critical habitat units with

a “no effect” determination for the Oregon spotted frog based on the various protective

determined that the effects on the species were covered by a 2016 Biological Opinion

For the gray wolf, BLM made a “may affect, not likely to adversely affect”

measures would minimize the impacts to denning gray wolves, and determined that the
action’s effects on the species were covered by a 2018 programmatic gray wolf informal

consultation which analyzed all land management activities within the Lakeview District,
and which culminated in FWS’s concurrence.215
KS Wild has not addressed these analyses and conclusions or BLM’s related

CONCLUSION
Based on the above, we hold that KS Wild failed to carry its burden to establish
any clear error of law or demonstrable error of fact in BLM’s April 5, 2019, Decision
broadening the scope of the KFRA’s invasive species management program. KS Wild has
not shown that the Decision violates the procedural requirements of NEPA, is
inconsistent with the governing resource management plan, or that BLM violated the
ESA. Accordingly, we affirm BLM’s Decision.

text:
MAY 0 1977
76-608 : Fish and Wildlife Service
FRANK AND RENE LOCK : Special Use Permit
: Appeal Dismissed
By letter dated January the Acting Regional Director,
Fish and Wildlife Service Department of the Interior, Denver,
Colorado, informed Frank Lock, appellant herein, that a special use
permit for grazing on the UL Bend-Bowdoin National Wildlife Refuge
would not be issued to him for calendar year 1976. The denial was
based on alleged permit violations which had occurred in previous
years. The original notification was returned unclaimed, but a sub
sequent notification by date of February 18, 1976, was received by
appellant Rene Lock, though the actual date of receipt is in
controversy.
The letter of January 9 declared that "Title 50, Code of Fed
eral Regulations, Section 29.22, makes reference to appeal proce
dures which are available should you desire to pursue an appeal."
By letter dated march 22, appellants filed a notice of appeal
from the decision of the Acting Regional Director.
On April 21, 1976, appellants filed a statement of reasons in
support of the appeal with this Board and requested that the board
refer the case to the Hearings Division for the assignment of an
administrative law judge who would hold a fact-finding hearing.
See 43 CFR 4.41b.
In a submission of 14, 1976, the Office of the Field
Solicitor moved that the Board dismiss the appeal of Frank and
Rene Lock on the ground, inter that the appeal was not prop
erly before the Board. Inasmuch as we believe that there is merit
to the position of the Solicitor, we hereby grant the motion and
dismiss the appeal.
The regulation cited by the Acting Regional Director in his
letter of January 9, 50 CFR 29.22, states, in relevant part:

76-608
An appeal may be taken from any final disposition
of the Regional Director, to the Director, U.S. Fish
and Wildlife Service, and, from the latter's decision
to the Secretary of the Interior. Such appeals may
be taken pursuant to 43 CFR Parts 1840 and 1850 except
that (a) a ll references to the "Director" or "Director,
Bureau of Land Management," are changed to Director,
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service The above proce
dures for hearing and appeals, 30 provided and amended,
are hereby adopted as procedures for hearings and
appeals by said U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.
This regulation was originally promulgated as proposed rule
making on June 20, 1969, 34 FR 9680, and was adopted on December 19,
1969, 34 FR 19907. Parts 1840 and 1850 of 43 CFR at that time pro
vided detailed regulations governing the taking of appeals from
decisions officers of the Bureau of Land Management and proce
dures to be utilized in hearings arising out of such appeals.
Under the procedures then in force, appeals from adverse decisions
by officials were first taken to the Director, BLM, where they
were processed by the Office of Appeals and Hearings. Appeals from
decisions of the Office of Appeals and Hearings could then be taken
to the Secretary. Appeals to the Secretary were normally decided
by the Assistant Solicitor for Public Lands.
Motivated in part by a concern that the appellate procedure
raised questions concerning a combination of functions within the
Office of the Solicitor, the Department, effective July 1,
established the Office of Hearings and Appeals consisting of the
Director and various Boards of Appeal. 35 FR 10012 (June 18,
1970). Parts 1840 and 1850 were amended to reflect these changes.
Part 1840 now reads, in relevant part: "For special procedural
rules applicable to appeals from decisions of Bureau of Land
Management officers or of law judges, within the
jurisdiction of the Board of Land Appeals, Office of Hearings
and Appeals, see Subpart E of Part 4 of this title. * *
43 CFR 1840.1." The hearing regulations, 43 CFR 1850, were
similarly changed.
With exceptions, the regulation now in effect establishes
a procedure in which persons appealing from a decision of the
Regional Director must first appeal to the Director. Appeals
taken from adverse decisions of the Director are then properly
considered by the Office of Hearings and Appeals. Thus, the
procedure is parallel to the procedure utilized to obtain review
of decisions of the Conservation Division, Geological Survey,
as well as the Bureau of Indian Affairs in matters concerning
mineral permits and leases. See 30 CFR 290 and 30 CFR 221.66,
250.81.

Unfortunately, the subject matter of the instant case falls
within the exceptions. Regulation 50 CFR 29.22 does not, by its
terms, apply herein. That regulation is found in subpart B of
Part 29, which only applies to rights-of-way. the proposed
rulemaking published on June 20, 1969, listed the change under the
heading "Rights-of-way Regulations." Moreover, nothing
50 CFR 29.22 lends itself to an interpretation that it was to
apply to other subparts within Part 29. For example, "Regional
Directors" is not defined in either subpart A or C of Part 29, nor
is the position even mentioned in these two subparts. All refer
ences to the Regional Director occur only in subpart B. Yet, a
reading of 50 CFR 29.22 makes it clear that the decisions which
are subject to an appeal to the Director, are those of the
Regional Director. We are forced to hold, therefore, that nothing
in 50 CFR 29.22 grants this Board jurisdiction over the instant
Nor can we find any other source by which this Board would
acquire jurisdiction over the instant appeal. While 43 CFR 4.1(3)
provides a very general grant of authority to the Board to decide
"finally for the Department appeals to the head of the Department
from decisions rendered by officials relating to the
use and disposition of public lands their resources," the terms
of 43 CFR limit the grant of the right to appeal to persons
adversely affected "by a decision of an officer of the Bureau of
Land or of an administrative law judge." Thus, absent
a specific grant of a right to appeal, such as is provided in
30 CFR 290 and 50 CFR 29.22, persons adversely affected by deci
sions of departmental officials other than those in the Bureau
of Land Management cannot seek review of the adverse decision
before this Board. The appeal, therefore, must be dismissed.
Accordingly, pursuant to the authority delegated to the Board
of Land Appeals by the Secretary of the 43 CFR 4.1, the
appeal is dismissed.
/s/ Newton
Newton Frishberg
Chief Judge
We concur:
Stuebing S/ Douglas E.
Edward W. Stuebing Douglas E. Henriques
Administrative Judge Judge

ORDER
J.R. Simplot Company (Simplot) appeals from four March 20, 2017, decisions of the
Idaho State Office, Bureau of Land Management (BLM), rejecting Simplot’s objections to
certain readjustments to the terms and conditions of Federal phosphate leases IDBL-
055894, IDBL-056009, IDI-000257, and IDI-000003.1
Because the facts and legal issues in each of these appeals are similar –
Simplot challenges the same readjusted language in each of its appeals – we consolidate
them.2 We set aside and remand BLM’s decisions in part and affirm BLM’s decisions in part.
For ease of understanding, unless otherwise stated, specific facts, such as dates, and
citations to pleadings, refer to those in the record for IBLA 2017-171.
SUMMARY
BLM issues phosphate leases under the Mineral Leasing Act (MLA) for an initial
20-year term. At the end of each 20-year period, BLM has broad authority to prescribe
reasonable readjustment of the terms and conditions of a phosphate lease, unless
otherwise provided by law. Here, BLM proposed various readjustments to phosphate
1 We docketed the appeals as follows: IDBL-055894, docketed as IBLA 2017-171;
IDBL-056009, docketed as IBLA 2017-172; IDI-000257, docketed as IBLA 2017-173; and
IDI-000003, docketed as IBLA 2017-174.
2 43 C.F.R. § 4.404. Citations to the Code of Federal Regulations are to the most recent
version, published in 2019.
1

IBLA 2017-171, et al.
leases and Simplot’s predecessor in interest filed objections, which BLM rejected between
eight and nine years later.
In its appeals, Simplot argues that BLM’s decisions violate the Administrative
Procedure Act (APA) because of BLM’s delay in issuing them and that they also violate the
Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA) by
imposing strict liability on Simplot. These precise issues were raised and addressed by the
Board in Nu-West Industries, Inc., and we follow that decision here. First, because nothing in
the MLA, BLM’s implementing regulations, or the APA requires BLM to respond to a lessee’s
objections to lease readjustments within any particular time frame, we reject Simplot’s
argument that BLM’s delay violated the APA. Second, we set aside BLM’s inclusion of one
challenged readjusted term – a broad indemnification clause – because its plain language
does not comport with BLM’s intent. Finally, we affirm BLM’s inclusion of the other
challenged readjusted term because it does not shift liability in violation of CERCLA.
BACKGROUND
A. BLM’s Authority to Reasonably Readjust Phosphate Lease Terms and Conditions
BLM issues phosphate leases under the MLA, which provides that lands containing
phosphate deposits “shall be leased under such terms and conditions as are herein
specified.”3 Phosphate leases are issued for an initial 20-year term and may continue “so
long thereafter as the lessee complies with the terms and conditions of the lease.”4 At the
end of each 20-year period, BLM has broad authority to readjust a phosphate lease under
the MLA: the bureau may prescribe “reasonable readjustment of the terms and conditions
[of a phosphate lease] . . . unless otherwise provided by law . . . .”5
B. BLM’s Proposed Readjustments to Simplot’s Phosphate Lease IBDL-055894 and
Simplot’s Objections
Effective December 1, 1948, BLM issued Phosphate Lease IBDL-055894 to Simplot.6
The Lease consists of 200 acres of private surface and Federal minerals in the State of
Idaho.7 Under Section 3 of the Lease, the Department of the Interior reserved the “right to
readjust” the terms and conditions of the Lease at the end of the 20th year, and thereafter

C. The Lease Readjustments at Issue
In each of its appeals, Simplot raised identical objections to the following readjusted
terms of its phosphate leases:

DISCUSSION
The Board addressed the same challenged readjusted lease terms in Nu-West
Industries, Inc.20 In this Order we incorporate by reference and adopt the reasoning and
conclusions in that decision.
A. Standard of Review and Burden of Proof
As noted above, BLM has broad authority to readjust phosphate leases issued under
the MLA.21 This Board has stated that, in a lease readjustment, “a lessee has only one
existing right: the right to accept or reject the continuation of [its] lease beyond a 20-year
period under such reasonable terms as the Secretary deems proper.”22 Thus, under the
MLA, any readjustment must comport with the law and be reasonable.23 As we have
explained, BLM must exercise its authority to readjust a lease in compliance “with the
requirements of law and standards of reasonableness” such that a lease does not contain
provisions that “are unacceptable because they are arbitrary, capricious, or an abuse of
discretion.”24 It is therefore an appellant’s burden to demonstrate that the readjusted terms
it challenges “are unreasonable or are otherwise arbitrary, capricious, or an abuse of
discretion.”25

B. Simplot’s Arguments on Appeal
On appeal, Simplot argues that each of BLM’s decisions rejecting P4’s objections to
its Lease readjustments violates the APA because of the delay between Simplot’s objections
and BLM’s decision.26 Simplot also argues that each of BLM’s decisions violates CERCLA.27
C. BLM’s Delay in Issuing its Decisions
Simplot complains that the nine-year delay between P4’s objections to its readjusted
Lease and BLM’s decision rejecting those objections violates the APA and renders BLM’s
decisions unlawful.28 In support of its argument, Simplot states that the BLM Decision
“neglects to mention or acknowledge that the proposed readjustments . . . were made
nearly nine years ago,” and “offers no explanation or justification” for BLM’s delay.29
Simplot makes the same argument with respect to BLM’s other decisions.
We addressed this issue in Nu-West, noting that neither the MLA nor BLM’s
implementing regulations require BLM to respond to a lessee’s objections to phosphate
lease readjustments within any particular time frame.30 We explained that while the
regulations impose a 60-day time period in which a lessee must object to proposed lease
readjustments, they do not specify a time for when BLM must respond to any objections,
stating only that BLM “will issue a decision in response.”31 We held that BLM’s delay did not
violate the law because BLM is not required to respond to lessee’s objections to phosphate
lease readjustments within any particular time frame.32 We also explained that Nu-West’s
reliance on the APA was misplaced since the statute’s provision requiring Federal courts to
“compel agency action unlawfully withheld or delayed,” cited by Nu-West, does not apply to
the Board.33
Simplot has failed to cite to any law or precedent in support of its position, and we
see no reason to deviate from our conclusion in Nu-West. We therefore conclude, as we did
in Nu-West, that BLM’s delay in issuing its decisions did not violate the law applicable to
phosphate lease readjustments.

D. Simplot’s CERCLA Arguments
At the heart of Simplot’s appeals is its argument that through the Lease
readjustments, BLM has unilaterally imposed strict liability on the company for the impacts
of all operations under its phosphate leases in violation of CERCLA.34 Again, Simplot’s
arguments are the same as those it made in Nu-West.
More specifically, Simplot argues that the readjusted language in Sections 12
(Indemnification) and 14(a) (Allocation of Response Costs and Natural Resources
Damages) imposes strict liability on Simplot in violation of CERCLA.35 Simplot further
argues that the readjusted language in Section 14(a) violates Simplot’s right to contribution
under CERCLA by requiring “that Simplot agree to be responsible for all costs resulting
from any release or the threat of a release of hazardous substances, pollutants,
contaminants, petroleum, or oil on or from the leased area irrespective whether that
release or threat of release was in any manner caused by Simplot.”36
We address these arguments below.
1. The Indemnification Clause in Section 12 Is Unreasonable Because Its Language
Does Not Comport with BLM’s Intent
Simplot argues that Section 12 of the readjusted leases, the indemnification clause,
is unlawful under CERCLA because it imposes strict liability on Simplot, and this Board has
already ruled that this exact clause is unreasonable.37
Simplot is correct that we have previously addressed this same indemnification
clause in other cases involving challenges to BLM phosphate lease readjustments, most
recently in Nu-West, which the Board issued while the present appeals were pending.
There, we found that the indemnification clause “may well impose strict or no fault
liability,” and re-affirmed the Board’s previous ruling in J.R. Simplot Co.38
In J.R. Simplot Co., we concluded that this same clause was unacceptable and flawed
because it would not be reasonable “for BLM to be held harmless for its mistakes or for [the
lessee] to be held liable to BLM for claims over which it has or had no control, culpability,
34 42 U.S.C. §§ 9601-9675; see United States v. Bestfoods, 524 U.S. 51, 55 (1998) (“‘CERCLA is
a comprehensive statute that grants the President broad power to command government
agencies and private parties to clean up hazardous waste sites.’”) (quoting Key Tronic Corp.
v. United States, 511 U.S. 809, 814 (1994)).

or responsibility.”39 We therefore held that “BLM cannot impose strict or no-fault liability
under Section 12 . . . .”40 But in J.R. Simplot Co., we did not strike the offending language.
Instead, we instructed that “BLM must either interpret and apply [that language] consistent
with [the Board’s] decision or revise that provision.”41
In response to the Board’s decision in J.R. Simplot Co., BLM issued Instruction
Memorandum (IM) No. 2008-096, specifying that BLM will not “use an indemnification
provision that was, or will be, added to a solid mineral lease in a lease readjustment to
impose liability on the lessee for damages caused by the BLM’s actions” and that BLM’s
policy “is not to treat the indemnification provision as a ‘strict liability’ provision.”42 In the
IM, BLM explained that, consistent with the Board’s ruling, BLM would not interpret and
apply the indemnification provision “so as to require the lessee to hold the BLM harmless
for damages caused by the BLM’s actions. The indemnification provision should not be
interpreted or applied to hold solid mineral lessees liable for claims over which the lessees
have or had no control, culpability, or responsibility.”43
In reliance on the Board’s ruling in J.R. Simplot Co. and its IM, BLM continued to
include the language of Section 12 in readjusted phosphate leases but interpreted that
language so as not to impose strict liability on lessees. This is what BLM did in the decisions
challenged in Nu-West and in the decisions now on appeal: BLM included Section 12 as a
readjusted term of Simplot’s phosphate leases, and, in rejecting P4’s objection to that
readjusted term, BLM explained that it was acting consistent with the J.R. Simplot Co.
decision and the IM.44 BLM therefore argues on appeal, as it did in Nu-West, that its
approach should be upheld because it is consistent with IBLA precedent.45
In Nu-West we confirmed our determination in J.R. Simplot Co. that the plain
language of Section 12 impermissibly imposes strict liability on a lessee in violation of
CERCLA, but found that the numerous other objections to BLM’s inclusion of Section 12 in
other readjusted phosphate leases, like those at issue in this appeal, dictated a different
resolution. We observed that at the time of our decision in J.R. Simplot Co.,

administrative adjudicatory process. The gap between the language in Section

language (not imposing strict liability) has created unnecessary confusion and

Rather than leave the Section 12 language intact, as we did in J.R. Simplot Co., we struck
Section 12 as unreasonable because it did not comport with BLM’s intent, setting aside and
remanding to BLM its decisions to include readjusted Section 12 in the phosphate leases.47
We follow Nu-West here and adopt the same reasoning and result with respect to the leases
that are the subject of this consolidated appeal. We therefore set aside and remand BLM’s
decisions to include Section 12 in Simplot’s readjusted leases.
2. The Cost Allocation Provision in Section 14(a) Does Not Improperly Impose Strict
Liability on Simplot
We turn now to Simplot’s objection to Section 14(a) of its readjusted leases. Section
14(a) allocates the costs of remediating hazardous substances under CERCLA, as well as
certain substances exempt from CERCLA, i.e., petroleum and oil. It provides that Simplot
will pay for or reimburse the United States for all response costs related to the release of
hazardous and other substances from activities undertaken by Simplot on its leases,
including “costs and damages accruing to the United States relating to such activities.”
Simplot asserts Section 14(a) prospectively imposes liability on the company for
activities not under its control and prospectively releases the United States from its own
potential liabilities, and therefore is inconsistent with CERCLA.48 According to Simplot, the
cost allocation provision is an improper attempt to contractually place the entire financial
burden for any environmental response actions relating to the leased lands on Simplot,
regardless of fault or statutory liability.49
In support of its argument, Simplot first states that BLM’s imposition of Section
14(a) in its readjusted leases is inconsistent with our ruling in J.R. Simplot Co. that BLM may
not impose strict liability on a lessee through unilateral lease readjustment under the
MLA.50 Simplot argues that the first sentence of Section 14(a) “goes well beyond CERCLA’s
admittedly broad reach by prospectively imposing liability on Simplot for actions not
46 Nu-West, 192 IBLA at 155.
47 Id.
48 SOR at 5.
49 Id. at 6.
50 Id.
9

IBLA 2017-171, et al.
caused by Simplot nor under Simplot’s control.”51 Simplot argues that the first sentence
does not address the reimbursement of costs but instead asks Simplot to be responsible for
all costs resulting from any release or the threat of release of hazardous substances,
pollutants, contaminants, petroleum, or oil on or from the leased area irrespective of
whether that release or threat of release was in any manner caused by Simplot.52
The Board addressed language identical to that in Section 14(a) in
J.R. Simplot Co., where we concluded that this was cost allocation language that “does not
shift liability but imposes an obligation on [the lessee] to indemnify the Government for
certain costs.”53 We found that the scope of the cost allocation clause was narrower than
the broad indemnification clause we found to be flawed since it limited allocated costs “to
those arising out of ‘activities undertaken by the lessee,’ as determined by ‘records on file
with BLM.’”54 Further, we considered BLM’s role as protector of public lands entrusted to
its care and concluded that there was no error in BLM requiring the lessee to reimburse the
Government for its costs in responding to releases arising out of the lessee’s activities on its
Federal lease.55 We therefore found that the provision was permitted under CERCLA and
reasonable to include in the readjusted lease.56 In Nu-West, also involving similar
challenges to identical Section 14(a) language, we followed the J.R. Simplot Co. analysis and
conclusion.57
Simplot’s argument rests on reading the first sentence of Section 14(a) in isolation.
As we concluded when addressing a similar argument in Nu-West, such a reading results in
a characterization of Section 14(a) that is overbroad.58 Similar to the arguments made in
Nu-West, Simplot’s assertion that Section 14(a) makes it liable for paying the costs of all
environmental response actions relating to the leased lands does not account for the
second sentence of Section 14(a), which specifies that the requirement that the lessee
reimburse the United States applies to “response costs and natural resource damages
based upon, arising out of, or in any way relating to, activities undertaken by the
lessee, . . . on the leased area . . . and includes but is not limited to, costs and damages
accruing to the United States related to such activities.”59 In Nu-West we further stated that,
as the Board found in J.R. Simplot Co., this sentence “limits costs subject to allocation to
those arising out of ‘activities undertaken by the lessee.’”60 Thus, Section 14(a) is more

57 Nu-West, 192 IBLA at 158.
58 Id. at 159.

IBLA 2017-171, et al.
limited than claimed by Simplot, and, consistent with our analysis and decision in Nu-West,
we reject its arguments to the contrary.
We therefore reaffirm our conclusions in J.R. Simplot Co. and Nu-West that the
provision is a reasonable lease readjustment under the MLA.
CONCLUSION
Simplot’s objections to the readjusted Sections 12 and 14(a) of the leases at issue in
this consolidated appeal have been previously addressed by the Board in Nu-West. For the
reasons stated in that decision and in this Order, we hold that BLM’s delay in issuing its
decisions did not violate the APA; we set aside and remand BLM’s decisions to include
Section 12 in the readjusted leases; and we affirm BLM’s decisions with respect to
readjusted Section 14(a).
Therefore, pursuant to the authority delegated to the Board of Land Appeals by the
Secretary of the Interior,61 we set aside and remand BLM’s decisions to the extent they
include Section 12 in Simplot’s readjusted leases, and affirm BLM’s decisions with respect
to all other aspects of the decisions challenged by Simplot.

ORDER
Walter Wilkins and Judith Humphrey have appealed from and requested a stay
of a December 19, 2006, decision of the Alaska State Office, Bureau of Land
Management (BLM). That decision declared the Perseverance Mining Claim
(AA-051097) forfeited for failure to pay the $125 per claim maintenance fee or to
a Maintenance Fee Payment Waiver Certification (Waiver Certification) on or before
September 1, 2006, for the 2007 assessment year. Appellants also request an
evidentiary hearing to resolve material issues of fact. Due to a lack of corroborating
evidence to support appellants' assertions, the request for a hearing is denied For
the following reasons, BLM's decision is affirmed.
Under 30 U.S.C. § 28f(a) (2000),1 the holder of an unpatented mining claim,
or tunnel site is required to pay a maintenance fee for each claim or site on
or before September 1 of each year for the years 2004 through 2008. See 43 C.F.R.

Congress, specifically by the Department of the Interior and Related Agencies
Appropriations Act, 2002, Pub. L. No. 107-63, 115 Stat. 414, 418-19 (2001)
(requiring the payment of the claim maintenance fee on or before September 1 of
each year for the years 2002 and 2003), and the Department of the Interior and

The failure to pay the claim maintenance fee "shall conclusively constitute a
forfeiture of the unpatented mining claim, mill or tunnel site by the claimant and the
claim shall be deemed null and void by operation of law." 30 U.S.C. § 28i (2000); see
43 C.F.R. §§ 3830.91(a), 3835.92(a). Congress, however, provided the Secretary'
with discretion to waive the fee for a claimant who certified in writing that on the
date the payment was due, the claimant and all related parties held not more than
mining claims, mill sites, or tunnel sites, or any combination thereof, on public
lands and had performed assessment work required under the Mining Law of 1872,
for the preceding assessment year ending at noon on September 1 of the calendar '
year in which payment of the claim maintenance fee is due. 30 U.S.C. § 28f(d)(l)
(2000); see Audrey Bradbury, 160 IBLA 269, 273-74 (2003). BLM implemented this
statute with a regulation that requires a claimant to file "BLM's waiver certification
form on or before September 1 of each assessment year for which you are seeking a
waiver." 43 C.F.R. § 3835.10(a).
Appellants contend that the claim holder, Walter Wilkins, timely filed a
Certification via hand delivery to the BLM Alaska State Office in August 2006, as was
his practice every year since he obtained the mining claim. Statement of Reasons
(SOR) at 2; SOR Ex. A at 2-3. The case record contains no evidence that Wilkins
filed a Waiver Certification, and appellants admit that they cannot proffer a copy
the document because, they assert, Wilkins either received and lost his date-stamped
copy, or he never received a date-stamped copy. Petition for Stay (Petition) Ex A
at 2; SOR Ex. A at 2.
The absence of a legally significant document from BLM's public records gives
rise to the presumption that it was never filed with BLM, since Federal Government
employees are presumed to have properly performed their official duties and not lost
or misplaced such a document. John J. 165 IBLA 265, 270 (2005), and
cases cited therein. This "presumption of regularity" can be rebutted, but the burden
of proof is placed on an appellant to offer evidence that the required document was
filed. Lewis v. Bureau of Land Management, 150 IBLA 76, 81 (1999).
Appellants attempt to rebut the presumption of regularity. Counsel for
appellants makes allegations about the general inadequacy of the Alaska State Office
to handle receipt of filings, and indicates that he has filed a request for documents
pursuant to the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), 5 U.S.C. § 554 (2000), to obtain
evidence supporting his allegations. SOR Ex. B; SOR Ex. 1. Furthermore, appellants

submit Wilkins' previously filed Waiver Certifications for the Perseverance claim to
demonstrate the regularity of his submissions. SOR Exs. 2-11.
Even assuming, arguendo, that appellants succeed in obtaining evidence that
inconsistencies have occurred in BLM's business practice, that evidence would not
suffice to demonstrate that a mistake was made in this instance. The Board has held
that "the presumption of regularity has never proceeded on the assumption that
errors are not made in the normal course of the administration of official functions,"
but rather, the presumption reigns in those cases where it cannot be rebutted.
Bureau Land Management v. Carlo, 133 IBLA 206, 210 (1995). To succeed,
appellants' assertions at page 4 of the SOR would have to be supported with evidence
that the Alaska State Office has either "general procedures ... so susceptible to error
that no inference of correct handling could properly arise or that the manifest record
of specific error establishes the level of error requires the abandonment of
any inference of Id: Such woeful conditions, if recently developed,
would no doubt be reflected in a surge of appeals specifically challenging the Alaska
State Office's handling of documents, and no such surge has occurred. If appellants
contend that the BLM Alaska State Office has always maintained such conditions,
that contention is refuted by their own submission of Wilkins' 10 consecutive Waiver
Certifications which were properly accepted and filed by BLM staff.
As for the regularity with which Wilkins submitted his Waiver Certifications,
the documents submitted by appellants show that 2 of the 10 filings were incorrectly
labeled "AA051017" and "AA051019" instead of AA051097.2 Moreover, while
Wilkins' practice was to retain a date-stamped copy of his Waiver Certification every
previous assessment year, he neglected to do so for the 2006 assessment year. Those
irregularities notwithstanding, the Board has held that even a perfect record of
compliance does not necessarily demonstrate that an individual must have complied
in a subsequent instance. F. Owen, 31 IBLA 24, 28 (1977). Wilkins' prior
compliance does not constitute evidence negating the absence of his Waiver
Certification from the case record.
Appellants request an evidentiary hearing under 43 C.F.R. § 4.415, suggesting
that whether or not Wilkins filed a Waiver Certification constitutes a material issue of
fact under that regulation. Although appellants present no corroborative evidence to
support their assertion, they further suggest that no such evidence is needed to
warrant a hearing in light Bureau Land Management v. Carlo. Appellants fail to

uncorroborated statements, even where placed in affidavit form, to

I. Burden of Proof
A party may appeal to this Board from an ALJ’s order granting or denying a
petition for stay of a final grazing decision.27 To prevail on appeal, the party must
demonstrate error in the ALJ’s order.28 Specifically, the party must demonstrate that the
ALJ committed a material error of law or fact or failed to demonstrate a rational
connection between the facts found and the decision made.29
II. Appellants Have Not Demonstrated That the ALJ Erred in Denying the Petitions
for Stay

success on the merits criterion and determined that Appellants had “raised significant

ruled that Appellants had not satisfied this criterion.31 Based upon this ruling, the ALJ
denied the petitions for stay without considering the other two stay criteria.32

of affected members of the public to participate in the agency’s decision-

Federal court case law, which the Board has adopted, provides that “a
procedural violation of NEPA is not itself sufficient to establish irreparable
injury.”[124]
On appeal, the Districts recognize that an alleged violation of NEPA alone does
not establish irreparable harm.125 But the Districts argue that an alleged NEPA violation
coupled with an environmental injury does.126 The Districts further contend that
environmental injuries from the fencing changes establish irreparable harm given the
ALJ’s suggestion that BLM failed to comply with NEPA in analyzing the fencing
changes.127 In support, the Districts assert the following environmental injuries from the
fencing changes: injuries to the range from removing (and potentially replacing)
fences,128 injuries from “the effects of electrifying the fences,”129 and injuries to the range

constitute irreparable harm. But we have rejected this notion.131 For example, we have
ruled that environmental injuries caused by pipeline construction were not irreparable

8 n.2 (asserting similar injuries to the range will occur if the Districts prevail on appeal
and the fences are reconstructed).
129 Id. at 8.
130 Id. at 8-9.
131 W. Watersheds Project v. BLM, 195 IBLA at 131-32 (ruling that “not . . . all
environmental injury is automatically irreparable”).
132 Heal Utah, 191 IBLA 103, 107 & n.28 (2017).
133 Id.
20

IBLA 2023-0048 et al.
Here, the ALJ ruled, in line with our precedent, that the Districts’ asserted
environmental injuries from the fencing changes did not constitute immediate and
irreparable harm based upon findings that the asserted injuries were either “short-term
and temporary”134 or unsupported.135 Because the Districts have not rebutted these
findings, they have not demonstrated that the ALJ erred in ruling that the environmental
injuries from the fencing changes did not constitute immediate and irreparable harm.
CONCLUSION
The ALJ was not required to consider all four stay criteria, and Appellants have
not demonstrated error in the ALJ’s ruling that Appellants failed to show a likelihood of
immediate and irreparable harm. Accordingly, we affirm the ALJ’s Order denying
Appellants’ petitions for stay.

DAVID H. CHILES &
RIMROCK EXPLORATION & DEVELOPMENT, INC. (ON RECONSIDERATION)
IBLA 2020-333-1 Decided June 3, 2022
Motion for reconsideration of a Board Order reversing and remanding decisions
by the Colorado State Office, Bureau of Land Management, that declared certain lode
mining claims abandoned and void by operation of law. CMC-253250, et al.
Reconsideration granted; Board Order vacated except as to IBLA 2020-336, which
is unconsolidated and stands as the final decision of the Department; remaining BLM
decisions reversed. Francis Sidigu, 194 IBLA 276 (2019), Barton Coffman (On
Reconsideration), 190 IBLA 1 (2017), and David McCarty, 181 IBLA 224 (2011),
overruled to the extent inconsistent.
APPEARANCES: David H. Chiles, Grand Junction, Colorado, and Alan Chiles, President,
Rimrock Exploration and Development, Inc., Grand Junction, Colorado, for Appellants;
Adam B. Eckman, Esq., Office of the Regional Solicitor, U.S. Department of the Interior,
Lakewood, Colorado, for the Bureau of Land Management.
OPINION BY ADMINISTRATIVE JUDGE HAUGRUD
On September 22, 2020, the Board issued a dispositive Order in David H. Chiles, et
al., IBLA 2020-333 (2020 Order), in which the Board consolidated and resolved four
appeals filed on behalf of David Chiles, Colby Chiles, and Rimrock Exploration and
Development, Inc. (Rimrock). Appellants challenged decisions by the Bureau of Land
Management (BLM) declaring nine lode mining claims abandoned and void by operation
of law because the claimants had not timely filed notices of intent to hold them by
December 30, 2019.1 We held the filing of notices of intent to hold (NOIs) by December
1 The four appeals were docketed as follows: IBLA 2020-333, an appeal filed by David
Chiles concerning his J Bird #3, J Bird #4, and Prince Albert #4 mining claims, serial
198 IBLA 82

IBLA 2020-333-1
30, 2019, was required by rule (not by statute) and that BLM was required to give
Appellants notice and an opportunity to cure their noncompliance before BLM could
declare their claims abandoned and void. Because BLM had not provided an opportunity
to cure, we reversed BLM’s decisions.
BLM timely filed a motion for reconsideration of our 2020 Order.2 BLM seeks
reconsideration with respect to eight of the nine mining claims.3 BLM contends that our
2020 Order “conflicts with express statutory language and Board precedent” by deeming
the filing of the NOI to be a regulatory requirement subject to cure rather than a
statutory duty which results in automatic forfeiture.4
SUMMARY
The Board may reconsider a decision when a party shows “extraordinary
circumstances” that warrant reconsideration. Here, BLM points out that our 2020 Order
conflicts with existing Board precedent and that we failed to address that precedent in
our decision. Because the Board’s failure to address conflicting precedent constitutes an
extraordinary circumstance, we grant reconsideration, vacate the 2020 Order with
respect to all but one appeal, and re-examine the issues in view of the Board’s precedent.
Having reconsidered, we reach the same result as in the 2020 Order but with
further explanation of our rationale. In doing so, we overrule Francis Sidigu, 194 IBLA
276 (2019), Barton Coffman (On Reconsideration), 190 IBLA 1 (2017), and David
McCarty, 181 IBLA 224 (2011), to the extent they are inconsistent with this decision.
Each of these decisions held that the filing of the NOI is a statutory requirement of the
Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (FLPMA), not subject to cure, in the
year that a small miner fee waiver certification is filed when the maintenance fee was
paid the prior year. None of the decisions considered, however, that the FLPMA NOI
filing requirement had been modified by the subsequent enactment of the maintenance
fee statute, 30 U.S.C. § 28f.

by Alan Chiles as President of Rimrock concerning the company’s KU #5 and #6 mining
claims, CMC-254061 and CMC-254062; IBLA 2020-336, an appeal filed by Alan Chiles as
President of Rimrock concerning the company’s J Bird mining claim, CMC-291674; and
IBLA 2020-342, an appeal filed by Alan Chiles on behalf of Colby Chiles concerning
Prince Albert #1, #2, and #3 mining claims, CMC-254069 through CMC-254071.

Ultimately, while the interaction of FLPMA and the maintenance fee statute may
be interpreted in several ways, we conclude the Department has interpreted those
authorities through its implementing regulations in a manner which makes the NOI a
regulatory requirement under the circumstances here. As explained below, our decision
means the NOI that is required to be filed by 43 C.F.R. § 3835.15(a) or § 3835.14(b) is
regulatory, and therefore curable.
BACKGROUND
A. Statutory and Regulatory Overview
Since 1872, Federal law has required a mining claimant on public lands to do
something each year to maintain the validity of an unpatented lode or placer mining
claim. Precisely what is required has evolved over time, with the current regime
governed by the assessment work requirements of the Mining Law of 1872 as amended
(Mining Law),5 the filing requirements found in section 314 of FLPMA,6 and the
maintenance fee provisions that are now codified with the Mining Law.7 These statutory
requirements have been implemented by the Department through regulations
promulgated at 43 C.F.R. parts 3800-3870, primarily parts 3834-3836.
Under the current system, claimants, such as Appellants, who qualify as small
miners because they hold no more than a total of 10 claims, mill sites, or tunnel sites,
have the option of maintaining their mining claims in one of two ways each year. As
discussed in more detail below, a small miner may elect to either (a) timely pay an
annual maintenance fee8 or (b) timely file a fee waiver certification,9 perform assessment
work on the claim,10 and file an affidavit attesting to the work conducted on the claim.11
The exact compliance requirements for any given calendar year depend on what choice
the small miner made for compliance both in the current calendar year and the
preceding year. In this appeal, Appellants had paid the maintenance fee in the prior year
and decided to file a waiver certification the next year, a decision which required them
to also file an NOI in the same calendar year they filed the waiver.12 Briefly explaining

the evolution leading to the current regime is helpful to understanding the filing
requirements that applied to Appellants in this instance.
The Mining Law of 1872 included provisions requiring claimants of unpatented
placer or lode mining claims to perform at least $100 worth of labor and improvements
each year after the year of location.13 Until 1976, this annual assessment work
requirement was the only Federally imposed one for maintaining a mining claim on the
public lands. With the enactment of FLPMA in 1976, however, Congress added an annual
recording requirement for lode and placer claims. For those claims, FLPMA requires
mining claimants to file annually with the local recorder’s office and with BLM either an
NOI, an affidavit of assessment work documenting the completion of the required
assessment work, or a detailed report of the geological, geophysical, or geochemical
surveys done on the claim.14 In practical effect, FLPMA requires filing an affidavit of
assessment work or, if assessment work is deferred or otherwise not required for an
assessment year, an NOI.15
The required FLPMA document must be filed “each year following the calendar
year in which the said claim was located” and before December 31 of each year.16 The
failure to timely file the appropriate instrument with the recorder’s office and with BLM
as required by FLPMA “shall be deemed conclusively to constitute an abandonment of
the mining claim . . . by the owner,” thereby rendering the claim void and deemed
forfeited.17
Beginning in 1992, Congress began to replace these assessment work and FLPMA
filing requirements with a yearly maintenance fee payment. Originally termed a “rental

an annual FLPMA document results in the forfeiture of a mining claim); see also id. §
3830.5 (“Forfeit or forfeiture means the voidance or invalidation of an unpatented mining

‘forfeited’ have the same effect in these regulations.”).

IBLA 2020-333-1

exceptions that applied only to that time period,18 Congress subsequently created fee
provisions that extended past 1994, termed them “maintenance fees,” and established
the statutory regime currently found as amended at 30 U.S.C. §§ 28f-28k.19 Under these
provisions, mining claimants are required to pay an annual claim maintenance fee on or
before September 1 of each year.20 The claim maintenance fee is “in lieu of the
assessment work requirement contained in the Mining Law of 1872 (30 U.S.C. 28–28e)
and the related filing requirements contained in [FLPMA].”21 Failure to timely pay the
maintenance fee “shall conclusively constitute a forfeiture of the unpatented mining
claim . . . by the claimant and the claim shall be deemed null and void by operation of
law.”22
The Secretary of the Interior may, however, waive the maintenance fee for a
claimant who holds no more than a total of 10 mining claims, mill sites, or tunnel sites
and who timely files a small miner waiver certification by September 1 for the upcoming
assessment year.23 Unlike a mining claimant who pays the maintenance fee “in lieu of”
performing annual assessment work under the Mining Law and submitting related
FLPMA documents, a qualified claimant who files a small miner fee waiver certification
is still subject to fulfilling those statutory requirements.24 Accordingly, a claimant who
files a small miner waiver certification must perform assessment work on the claim
during the assessment year and file an affidavit on or before the December 30
immediately following the end of the assessment year, documenting the completion of
the required assessment work.25

The precise filing requirements for a given calendar year required by the
regulations implementing this statutory regime differ depending on the method of
compliance a small miner chooses from one year to the next. There are four possibilities
for existing mining claims. If a small miner paid the fee the previous year, and timely
pays the maintenance fee again in the current year (the “pay-pay” scenario), then no
FLPMA filing is required in the current calendar year.26 If the small miner filed a fee
waiver certification the previous year, and timely files a fee waiver certification again in
the current year (the “waiver-waiver” scenario), then the claimant must file an affidavit
of assessment work by December 30 of the current year attesting to completion of the
assessment work required by filing the prior year’s fee waiver certification.27 If a small
miner filed a fee waiver certification the prior year but decides to pay the maintenance
fee in the current year (the “waiver-pay” scenario), the claimant must still file the
affidavit of assessment work in the year of payment to show completion of the
assessment work required by filing the prior year’s fee waiver certification.28
The final scenario, the one at issue in this appeal, occurs when the small miner
has paid the maintenance fee in the prior year but decides to file a fee waiver
certification in the current year (the “pay-waiver” scenario). The Department’s
regulations have a specific provision governing this pay-waiver scenario, codified at 43
C.F.R. § 3835.15. The regulation provides that the claimant must make “a FLPMA filing,
in the form of a notice of intent to hold . . . , on or before December 30th immediately
following the submission of a waiver request.”29 The regulation also specifies that the
claimant must perform assessment work on the claim during the assessment year for
which the waiver applies and then file an affidavit of assessment work on or before the
December 30 immediately following the end of that assessment year.30
The foregoing regulatory requirements are not in dispute. The disputed issue
raised by BLM is whether filing the NOI in the pay-waiver scenario is required by FLPMA
(as BLM asserts) or is instead a regulatory requirement (as the Board concluded in its
2020 Order). The distinction is significant because the violation of a regulatory, but not
statutory, requirement is a curable defect.31 When a defect is curable, BLM must provide
the claimant with notice and an opportunity to cure the defect, and only if the claimant
fails to cure the defect within the time allotted will the affected mining claim be declared
forfeited.32

27 See id. § 3835.31(d)(3).
28 Id. § 3835.16(a).
29 Id. § 3835.15(a).

Finally, we note that the requirement to file an NOI may also arise with regard to
tunnel and mill sites,33 mining claims for which assessment work has been deferred or
waived,34 and newly recorded mining claims.35 Because all the mining claims for which
reconsideration has been sought are existing claims which do not fall into any of these
situations, we do not further discuss the filing requirements for these situations.
B. Factual and Procedural Overview
1. Events Leading to BLM’s Decisions and the Appeal to the Board
The essential facts are not in dispute.36 Except for the J Bird (CMC-291674) claim,
each of the claims was located in 2005, and for each one maintenance fees were paid
every year to maintain the claims through the assessment year ending in 2019. In August
2019, instead of paying the annual claim maintenance fees for the 2019-2020
assessment year, the Appellants filed maintenance fee waiver certifications for each of
the claims.
The J Bird claim, for which reconsideration has not been sought, differs because
of its later date of location. Appellant Rimrock recorded its location of the J Bird claim
with BLM in January 2019, and paid the required initial maintenance fee at the time of
recording. As with the other mining claims at issue, in August 2019 Rimrock filed a
maintenance fee waiver certification for the J Bird claim rather than pay the annual
maintenance fees for the upcoming 2019-2020 assessment year.
Soon after receiving the waiver requests, BLM sent out two notices – one to
Rimrock and one to claimant David Chiles – reminding them of the obligation to file an
NOI by December 30, 2019.37 The reminder notices addressed six of the nine claims at
issue.38 The notices had differently worded explanations, but both warned that failure to
file the NOI “on or before” the deadline will result in the mining claims being “forfeited

2. The Board’s 2020 Order
By Order dated September 22, 2020, the Board consolidated the appeals and
reversed all four BLM decisions. We recognized that Appellants had violated their duty to
file an NOI by December 30, 2019, but we concluded the duty was a regulatory one for
which BLM should have provided Appellants an opportunity to cure. We relied on the
terms of 30 U.S.C. § 28f(a), concluding that its “in lieu of” provision meant that
Appellant’s payment of the maintenance fee in 2018 had the effect of excusing them
from performing assessment work for the 2019 assessment year and filing a FLPMA
document at the end of calendar year 2019: “Since Appellants paid their claims’ annual
maintenance fees for the 2019 assessment year ‘in lieu of’ the related annual filing of a
FLPMA document for that assessment year, they were not required to make an annual
FLPMA filing by December 30, 2019.”47 Thus, we held the requirement to file an NOI
under these circumstances was a regulatory requirement imposed by 43 C.F.R. § 3835.15
rather than a statutory duty imposed by FLPMA. Because the failure to comply with a
regulatory requirement is curable, and BLM had not given Appellants notice and an
opportunity to cure their noncompliance with 43 C.F.R. § 3835.15, we reversed the BLM
decisions and remanded so that BLM could allow Appellants to cure their
noncompliance.48
3. BLM’s Motion for Reconsideration
On November 4, 2020, BLM timely filed a motion for reconsideration of our 2020
Order, contending that it “conflicts with express statutory language and Board
precedent” and that the Board should “reverse or vacate” the 2020 Order and “reinstate
and affirm BLM’s April 1, 2020, decisions.”49 However, BLM did not seek reconsideration
of our disposition of the J Bird claim.50

BLM asserts that the Board committed two interrelated errors in its 2020 Order.
First, and most fundamentally, BLM asserts the Board erred in deeming the filing of the
NOIs to be only a regulatory requirement of 43 C.F.R. § 3835.15 rather than a statutory

4. Supplemental Briefing Was Ordered
Upon reviewing the motion, the Board asked for supplemental briefing to be
certain it understood BLM’s interpretation of the governing statutes.56 We stated that the
Board’s 2020 Order was predicated on the view that payment of the maintenance fee is
in lieu of the claimant (a) performing assessment work in the upcoming assessment year
and (b) making a FLPMA filing following the end of that assessment year.57 We posited
that BLM instead seemed to believe that payment of the maintenance fee is in lieu of
making a FLPMA filing in the same calendar year as the payment since, under that
construction, the Appellants’ payment in 2018 would exempt them from a FLPMA filing
at the end of 2018 but would have no effect on the statutory requirement to make a
FLPMA filing in 2019 when the fee waiver certification was filed.58
We further explained the FLPMA filing consequences of those two differing
interpretations under the four claim maintenance scenarios that may arise with existing
mining claims.59 The interpretations lead to the same result when a claimant does not
change its method of claim maintenance from one year to the next. Under either
interpretation, no FLPMA filing is due under the pay-pay scenario, and a FLPMA filing is
always required under the waiver-waiver scenario.
But they differ in assessing what is a statutory filing duty when a claimant
switches compliance methods from one year to the next. We noted that, in addition to
the difference in the pay-waiver scenario, the two interpretations also impact the analysis

before December 30th immediately following the submission of a waiver

(waivable by small miners) that is “in lieu of the assessment work requirement contained

maintenance fee in the prior calendar year, which by virtue of § 28f(a) is “in lieu of” the
upcoming assessment year’s work requirement and the “related filing requirements” of

d. We overrule conflicting Board decisions
We recognize that our conclusion today is not consistent with the holdings of
three Board decisions which have expressly addressed the pay-waiver scenario: David
McCarty, 181 IBLA 224 (2011); Barton Coffman (On Reconsideration), 190 IBLA 1
(2017); and Francis Sidigu, 194 IBLA 276 (2019). Each decision involved the pay-waiver
scenario in which the claimant had failed to file an NOI by December 30 in the year a
maintenance fee waiver had been requested for the upcoming assessment year and
where the claimant had paid maintenance fees for the previous assessment year. In each
instance the Board held that FLPMA required the filing of an NOI and the failure to file it
rendered the mining claim void by operation of law, citing to the automatic
abandonment provision of section 314(c) of FLPMA.111 Our recent decision in Francis
Sidigu stated the legal premise succinctly: “The failure to file the notice of intent to hold
by the [December 30] deadline is not a curable defect and constitutes an abandonment
of the mining claim by the owner.”112
None of these decisions analyzed the effect of the “in lieu of” provision of
30 U.S.C. § 28f(a) on the FLPMA filing. The decision with the most significant discussion
of why an NOI was statutorily required, Barton Coffman (On Reconsideration), relied
exclusively on the position that FLPMA requires an annual filing after the year of
location, so any required FLPMA filing must be statutory:
In applying section 314(a) of FLPMA, the critical question is whether the
FLPMA filing in question is for a “year following the calendar year in which
the said claim was located.” In the present case, Appellants did not file a
notice of intent to hold their claim by December 30, 2014, a year following
the calendar year in which their claim was located. Thus, they did not meet
the annual filing requirement embodied in section 314(a) of FLPMA.[113]
But as discussed above, this formulation ignores the subsequent enactment of the
maintenance fee statute and its requirement that a maintenance fee payment be in lieu
of the assessment work required by the Mining Law and “the related filing requirements
contained” in section 314 of FLPMA.114 By failing to consider the effect of § 28f(a), the

addressing two mining claims, one of which involved a failure to file an NOI in the pay-
waiver situation. For that claim, the maintenance fee had been paid for the 2018
assessment year, then Sidigu timely filed a fee waiver certification for the 2019
assessment year, but Sidigu failed to file an NOI by December 30, 2018.116 Relying on
Barton Coffman (On Reconsideration) and citing 43 C.F.R. §§ 3835.15(a) and 3835.91,
the Board held that Sidigu automatically forfeited the claim when he failed to file the
NOI.117 The decision erred by relying on Barton Coffman (On Reconsideration) and
deeming the failure to be a noncurable statutory violation instead of a curable regulatory
one. Accordingly, we overrule both Francis Sidigu and Barton Coffman (On
Reconsideration) to the extent they are inconsistent with this decision.
David McCarty requires separate analysis because it involves the pay-waiver
scenario in the context of a “newly recorded” mining claim, which is governed by
43 C.F.R. § 3835.14 rather than § 3835.15. For newly recorded mining claims, the initial
claim maintenance fee is paid at the time of recording to cover the assessment year in
which the claim was located.118 The regulation allows a mining claimant to file a fee
waiver certification for the next assessment year, and it requires an NOI to be filed in the
same calendar year as the waiver.119 BLM recognizes that this NOI filing requirement is
regulatory in those situations where the claimant files the NOI in the same calendar year
in which the claim was located.120 That occurs when the mining claim is recorded, and
the fee waiver filed, before September 1 in a given year. The NOI is a regulatory
requirement in that circumstance because FLPMA by its express terms does not require
annual filings in the year of location.121
However, a new mining claim can also be located and recorded between
September 1 and December 31, which is the situation presented in McCarty. The mining
claim in McCarty was recorded, and the initial maintenance fee paid, in December
2008.122 In August 2009, McCarty timely filed a small miner fee-waiver certification, as
authorized by 43 C.F.R. § 3835.14, but he failed to file the required NOI by December

requires an annual filing after the year of location, and since an affidavit could not be

In view of our holding today, leaving unaddressed the holding in McCarty would
create a peculiar regulatory regime. It would mean, in the pay-waiver scenarios governed
by 43 C.F.R. §§ 3835.14 (for newly recorded claims) and 3835.15 (for existing claims),
that the requirement to file an NOI in the year the waiver is sought would be regulatory,
and curable, in all situations except for mining claims newly recorded the prior year
between September 1 and December 31. We do not believe this result follows the intent
of Congress or the Department. Although assessment work is not required in the
assessment year of location, we conclude that the initial claim maintenance fee is in lieu
of filing a FLPMA document for the assessment year covered by the payment, just as
payment of the maintenance fee is every other year. This conclusion is consistent with
Congress’s specific cross reference to 30 U.S.C. § 28f(a) in the subsection setting forth
the initial claim maintenance fee requirement.126 Accordingly, we conclude that the
Board erred in McCarty and overrule its implicit conclusion that the filing of the NOI in
that instance was a violation of a statutory, not regulatory, requirement. Because the
mining claim in McCarty was also forfeited by operation of law for other reasons, the
affirmance of BLM’s decision remains valid.
Our ruling today means the notice of intent to hold that is required to be filed in
the pay-waiver scenario by 43 C.F.R. § 3835.15(a) or § 3835.14(b) is regulatory, and
therefore curable. But the FLPMA document (typically an affidavit) required to be filed
in the waiver-pay scenario by 43 C.F.R. § 3835.16(a) is a non-curable statutory
requirement, as we have previously concluded.127

CONCLUSION
For the reasons discussed above, we order as follows:
1. BLM’s motion for reconsideration is granted, and the Board’s Order dated
September 22, 2020, issued in the four appeals consolidated as IBLA 2020-333 et al., is
vacated except as to IBLA 2020-336.
2. The appeal docketed as IBLA 2020-336, appealing BLM’s decision declaring
the J Bird mining claim (CMC-291674) void, is removed from consolidation. Because
BLM did not seek reconsideration of our disposition of that appeal, our previous holding
remains the final decision of the Department. As we previously held, BLM’s decision
declaring the J Bird claim to be void is reversed and the matter remanded to BLM to
provide the claimant an opportunity to cure. Our ruling in IBLA 2020-336 has no
precedential value.
3. We reverse BLM’s decisions declaring the eight mining claims at issue in
IBLA 2020-333, IBLA 2020-335, and IBLA 2020-342 to be abandoned and void. The
failure to file the notice of intent to hold as required by 43 C.F.R. § 3835.15(a)
constituted a regulatory violation for which the claimants should have been provided
notice and an opportunity to cure.
To allow for orderly consideration128 and implementation of our ruling, this
decision will not become effective until 45 days from the date of issuance. The Board will
not issue orders relying on this decision until it becomes effective.
